Welcome to the garden! Your assigned bed is marked with the number on your membership card. Some painted numbers have faded, so check the plan on the noticeboard if you are unsure. Add the arrangement to the noticeboard only with their agreement, so a request does not look like a job they have accepted.

Weeds without seed heads can go in the green compost bay. Put weeds with seed heads in the covered brown bin. If you are unsure whether a plant has set seed, leave it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. This is just a sorting precaution, not a judgment about anyone’s gardening.

Stewards are usually here on Saturday mornings. Check the noticeboard for the next session and any cancellation. We are glad you are here, and we would rather answer a small question before planting than help move a thriving crop out of somebody else’s bed.

We compared the current worksheet, which requires an operator to enter a blank reading for each sample, with a proposed worksheet that imports blank readings from the instrument log. The proposed worksheet is intended to reduce transcription. We assessed agreement between the corrected fluorescence values and the time required to produce them. The experiment did not include certified reference material, so it did not assess accuracy against a known true concentration.

Twenty-four aliquots from eight prepared solutions, with three aliquots per solution, were measured in one session in a fixed order by solution number. Both worksheets processed the same instrument readings. Each aliquot was measured once, so the worksheet comparison did not include independent repeats of the instrument signal. The operator completed the manual worksheet before the imported worksheet was generated and could not see the imported results during manual entry.

In the initial comparison, corrected values agreed to the instrument’s displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots. The three differences occurred in the final solution, where one blank entry had been copied into three rows of the manual worksheet. Inspection of the saved log showed that this entry was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows in the log, making the manual corrected values 0.2 units lower. After the initial comparison, we replaced the copied entry with the logged blank. The corrected values then agreed for all 24 aliquots at the displayed precision. This result reflects a subsequent correction, not agreement in the initial comparison.

The initial differences are consistent with a transcription error in this session. The three affected aliquots reflect one copied entry and do not establish three independent transcription errors. Only one operator used the worksheet, and that operator knew the comparison concerned data entry, so the observed error cannot be used to estimate a routine operator error rate. Agreement after correction supports the conclusion that the import applied the intended subtraction to these inputs. It does not establish agreement beyond the displayed precision or correct blank assignment in future instrument logs.

Producing the imported worksheet took four minutes, compared with eleven minutes for manual entry and checking. These timings excluded instrument operation and the later investigation of the discrepancy. The seven-minute saving applies to this session and its number of rows. Whether it persists when log formats change or an operator must resolve a missing blank was not measured.

response:
Returning keyboard focus to the same cell puts the cursor back. Does the user know where they are? This hypothetical study asked whether speaking the current row label when a note closes helps screen-reader users return to a table.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with the spoken cue and four with the existing version, which returns focus to the same cell without the cue. Six used the cue version first, and six used the existing version first. The two task sets used different tables. Within each order group, the assignment of tables to versions was reversed for half the participants.

We timed the interval from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside that interval. We calculated each participant’s mean completion time for each version, then took the median of those twelve means: 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. The three-second difference is between those medians, not the median of the twelve within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or performed a significance test.

Did the cue help users feel oriented? Nine participants said it did in the closing interview. Four of those nine also described occasions when it interrupted speech they were still listening to. The remaining three did not report an orientation benefit. None asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype, but participants were not asked to choose a default. Their responses do not establish that they wanted the cue enabled by default.

The task order reduced the alignment between version and practice, but it could not rule out learning effects. Some participants may have learned a search strategy in the first task set and carried it into the second. The study also leaves two scope questions open: how less experienced users would respond, and how the cue would work in large tables. We recruited only experienced users, and every table fit within one screen in the prototype.

The observations make an orientation benefit plausible for some users on these tasks. The interviews also suggest that added speech can compete with speech the user still wants to hear. That remains a design question even if a completion-time difference eventually proves reliable. A next version could make the cue interruptible, but we did not implement or test that behavior. The present timings provide no evidence for how an interruptible cue would perform.

## Question

Does a spoken location cue help users return to a table after opening a note?

## Method

We built a version that speaks the current row label when the note closes. The existing version returns keyboard focus to the same cell without the added cue. Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with each version. Six used the cue version first, and six used the existing version first. Different tables were used for the two sets of tasks. For half of each order group, the assignment of tables to versions was reversed.

We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside the timed interval.

## Results

The median of the twelve participant-level mean completion times was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. This compares two medians. It is not the median of the twelve within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision.

We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test, so we cannot say whether the difference is reliable.

In the closing interview, nine participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described occasions when the cue interrupted speech they were still listening to. The other three reported no orientation benefit. None of the twelve asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype. That is not the same as wanting it enabled by default, and participants were not asked to choose a default.

## Interpretation

The orientation reports make a benefit plausible for some users on these tasks. They also show that added speech can compete with speech already in progress. Whether the cue is worth those interruptions is a design question. It stays open even if the time difference later proves reliable.

A next version could make the cue interruptible. We did not implement or test that behavior in this study, so the timings above should not be read as evidence for it.

## Limitations

- Counterbalancing reduced the complete alignment between version and practice order, but it did not remove every learning effect. Some participants may have learned a search strategy in the first set of tasks and carried it into the second.
- All participants were experienced users. We did not recruit less experienced users, so we do not know how they would respond.
- The tables were short enough to fit on one screen in the prototype. The study does not establish performance on large tables.

**Does a spoken location cue help users return to a table after opening a note?**

**Summary.** We asked whether speaking the current row label when a note closes helps screen-reader users find their place again. The existing version returns keyboard focus to the same cell without the added cue. Twelve experienced screen-reader users each completed four tasks with each version. Participants' mean times were slightly lower with the cue, and most participants said it helped them feel oriented. Several also said it interrupted speech they were still listening to. We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test, so the timing difference is a description of this sample only.

**Design.** Six participants used the cue version first and six used the existing version first. The two sets of tasks used different tables, and for half of each order group we reversed which tables went with which version. We timed each task from the closing of the note to the activation of the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside the timed interval.

**Timing.** For each participant we took the mean completion time across their tasks with each version. The median of these twelve means was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. This is a difference between two medians, not the median of the twelve within-person differences. At the recorded precision, seven participants had a lower mean with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means.

**Interviews.** Nine participants said in the closing interview that the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described times when the cue interrupted speech they were still listening to. The other three did not report an orientation benefit, but none asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype. Does that mean they would want it on by default? We can't say. Participants were not asked to choose a default, and not asking for removal is a different response. These interview comments are self-reports and not measured performance.

**Limits.** The ordering scheme broke the complete alignment of version with practice, but it did not remove every possible learning effect. A participant may have learned a search strategy in the first set of tasks and carried it into the second. We recruited only experienced screen-reader users, so we do not know how less experienced users would respond. The prototype's tables were short enough to fit on one screen, so the study says nothing about large tables.

**What the product team can take from this.** Under these tasks, an orientation benefit is plausible for some users. The interviews also show that added speech can compete with speech a user is still listening to. That competition is a design question even if a time difference later proves reliable. A next version could make the cue interruptible. We did not implement or test that behavior here, so the timings above are not evidence for it. The next test should follow whether the cue arrives while a user is still listening, and not only how long the return to the table takes.

response:
The waiting list has grown, and the proposal to halve every returning gardener’s bed responds to a real concern: access to shared land should not depend on having joined years ago. There are twenty full beds and ten households waiting. But deciding how to share the land also means deciding how much opportunity gardeners have to keep crops through their growing cycle. I support dividing vacant beds first, while giving returning gardeners one more season in their present beds.

Four full beds will become vacant at the end of this season. Dividing them would create eight half beds for households on the waiting list. If every offer is accepted, two households would remain without a bed. That is a real shortfall, but the proposal would admit eight households without requiring every returning gardener to remove established planting at once.

Protecting established planting can also protect an established advantage. A perennial cannot give its gardener a permanent claim to shared land, and our membership agreement promises a bed for one season, with renewal decided annually. The reason to allow one more season is to give gardeners time to prepare for a change. The committee would publish the following season’s allocation rule before renewals open.

That rule should cover both returning and new members. A household accepting a half bed also needs to know whether beds will later be merged or moved. Otherwise, we risk passing the same uncertainty on to new gardeners. I do not yet favor a particular permanent bed size. We can agree on this transition while leaving that question open, provided we set a clear deadline for the next allocation rule.

Access needs must remain part of the allocation decision. Two of the twenty full beds are raised beds reserved for gardeners who need them, and neither is among the four becoming vacant. My proposal keeps that reservation and the existing access assessment unchanged. A standard half bed is not automatically a substitute for a raised bed, even if both are counted by area on the plan.

Starting with vacancies also has a practical drawback: all four are at the far end of the site, so all eight new households would begin in the same area. We could invite returning members to exchange locations voluntarily, but we cannot count on those exchanges. Nor should a new household have to negotiate a private favor to get a usable route to its bed. Before making offers, the committee should check the paths to the new half beds and report any access problem it cannot resolve.

For these offers, the waiting list would retain its current order. This preserves whatever disadvantages households faced in learning about the list, and that deserves attention. But changing the order during this allocation would introduce another contested decision without notice to those waiting. We can begin reviewing how the list is advertised now. Any future change to its order should be announced before it applies.

The meeting therefore has two costs to weigh. Under my proposal, two waiting households may receive no offer this season. Dividing every occupied bed immediately might create more places, but would disrupt established planting much more widely. I favor dividing the vacancies first and allowing one more season for the transition, with the remaining wait and the effect on existing crops both acknowledged.

The raised beds should stay outside this arithmetic. Two of the twenty full beds are raised beds reserved for gardeners who need them, and neither is among the four becoming vacant. My proposal keeps that reservation and leaves the existing access assessment unchanged. A standard half bed is not automatically a substitute for a raised bed, even if the plan counts their areas in the same way.

There is a practical objection to starting with vacancies. The four vacant beds are at the far end of the site, so all eight new households would begin in the same area. We could invite returning members to exchange locations voluntarily, but I do not want to count voluntary exchanges as a guaranteed part of the proposal. The committee should check the paths to the new half beds before making offers and report any access problem it cannot resolve.

The waiting list would keep its current order for these offers. I know that preserving this order also preserves whatever disadvantages people faced in learning about the list. Changing the order during this allocation would add another contested decision and give households no notice. A review of how the list is advertised can begin now, and any future change to the ordering should be announced before it applies.

This is a limited proposal with a visible cost: two waiting households may receive no offer this season. Dividing every occupied bed immediately might create more places, but it would spread the disruption much more widely. **Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\ge1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and put
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then \(d_n\ge0\) for every \(n\), and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\ge1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an \(N\ge1\) for which this tail is less than \(\varepsilon\).

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge0\).

To find the sum of the series, we first add its first \(N\) terms. Substituting the definition of \(d_n\), we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The intermediate terms cancel: each of \(a_2,\ldots,a_N\) appears once with each sign. Thus
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_n\to0\), this difference tends to zero. Hence the partial sums \(S_N\) tend to \(a_1\), which is precisely what it means for the series to converge to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\ge1\). For any integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular,
\[
\left|\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n-a_{N+1}\right|=a_{M+1}.
\]
As \(M\to\infty\), the right-hand side tends to zero. The finite sums of the tail therefore converge to \(a_{N+1}\), proving
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, given \(\varepsilon>0\), the assumption \(a_n\to0\) provides an integer \(K\ge1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\ge K\). Taking \(N=K\), we obtain
\[
0\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
The argument also includes zero terms and equal consecutive terms: neither cancellation nor the limit calculation requires strict decrease. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and put
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then \(d_n\geq 0\) for every \(n\), and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\geq 1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, this tail is less than any given \(\varepsilon>0\) when \(N\) is sufficiently large.

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\geq a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\geq 0\).

To find the sum of the series, we first add its first \(N\) terms. The intermediate terms cancel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
&=\sum_{n=1}^{N}(a_n-a_{n+1})\\
&=(a_1-a_2)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the distance from \(S_N\) to \(a_1\) is
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Given \(\varepsilon>0\), the assumption \(a_n\to 0\) provides an integer \(K\geq 1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\geq K\). For every \(N\geq K\), we therefore have
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
This proves that the partial sums tend to \(a_1\), which is exactly what it means for the series to converge to \(a_1\).

Now fix an integer \(N\geq 1\). For \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The distance between this finite sum and \(a_{N+1}\) is \(a_{M+1}\), which tends to zero as \(M\) increases. By the definition of an infinite series, this proves
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
Using the integer \(K\) chosen above, every \(N\geq K\) therefore satisfies
\[
0\leq \sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]

No strict decrease is needed: equal consecutive terms simply give \(d_n=0\). If \(a_1=0\), nonnegativity and monotonicity force every \(a_n\) to be zero, and the same identities apply. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0$. Put $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}$. Then every $d_n$ is nonnegative, the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$, and for every integer $N \ge 1$ its tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$. In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

*Nonnegativity.* Since the sequence is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$, so $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0$.

*Partial sums.* Fix integers $M > N \ge 1$. We compute two finite sums by telescoping. In each sum, the terms $-a_{k+1}$ from one summand cancel the terms $a_{k+1}$ from the next, so only the first and last terms survive.

For the first $N$ terms,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
&= (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}) \\
&= a_1 - a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the terms from $N+1$ through $M$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
&= (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) \\
&= a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

*Limits.* Let $M \to \infty$ in the first identity, which does not involve $M$, to get the partial sums of the whole series. Since $a_{N+1} \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$, the partial sums $\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n = a_1 - a_{N+1}$ converge to $a_1$. So the series converges, with sum $a_1$.

For the tail, fix $N$ and let $M \to \infty$ in the second identity. Since $a_{M+1} \to 0$, we get

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}.
$$

This is the claimed tail formula. It holds for every $N \ge 1$.

*Tail bound.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $a_k \to 0$, there is an index $K$ such that $a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. Set $N = \max(1, K)$. Then $N + 1 \ge K$, so

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.
$$

*Edge cases.* If $a_1 = 0$, then nonnegativity and monotonicity force $a_n = 0$ for all $n$, since $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$. The identities above still hold, with every term equal to zero. If $a_n = a_{n+1}$ for some $n$, then $d_n = 0$. The argument never needed a strict decrease, only $a_{n+1} \le a_n$.

response:
**Theorem.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0$. For $n\ge 1$, define
$$
d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}.
$$
Then:

1. $d_n \ge 0$ for every $n \ge 1$.
2. The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges, and its sum is $a_1$.
3. For every integer $N\ge 1$, the tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n$ converges and equals $a_{N+1}$.
4. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an integer $N\ge 1$ such that the tail after $N$ terms is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

**Step 1: Nonnegativity.** Because the sequence is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1}\le a_n$ for every $n\ge 1$. Therefore
$$
d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0.
$$

**Step 2: The partial sums telescope.** For each integer $M\ge 1$, let $S_M$ denote the $M$th partial sum,
$$
S_M = \sum_{n=1}^M d_n.
$$
Writing out the terms,
$$
S_M = (a_1-a_2) + (a_2-a_3) + \cdots + (a_{M}-a_{M+1}).
$$
Each interior term $a_k$ with $2\le k\le M$ appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so these cancel in pairs. Only the first and last terms survive:
$$
S_M = a_1 - a_{M+1}. \tag{1}
$$
For example, when $M=1$, (1) reads $d_1 = a_1-a_2$, which is the definition of $d_1$.

**Step 3: The series converges to $a_1$.** A series converges to $L$ exactly when its partial sums converge to $L$. Since $a_n\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$, we also have $a_{M+1}\to 0$ as $M\to\infty$. By (1),
$$
\lim_{M\to\infty} S_M = \lim_{M\to\infty}\bigl(a_1 - a_{M+1}\bigr) = a_1 - 0 = a_1.
$$
So $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges, with sum $a_1$. This step uses only the definition of convergence and the limit of $(a_n)$. It does not use nonnegativity.

**Step 4: The tail after $N$ terms.** Fix an integer $N\ge 1$. For $M>N$, the partial sums of the tail are
$$
T_M = \sum_{n=N+1}^M d_n = S_M - S_N.
$$
Applying (1) to $S_M$ and to $S_N$,
$$
T_M = \bigl(a_1 - a_{M+1}\bigr) - \bigl(a_1 - a_{N+1}\bigr) = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}. \tag{2}
$$
Equivalently, the terms $d_{N+1},\dots,d_M$ telescope to $a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}$ directly. As $M\to\infty$, $a_{M+1}\to 0$, so (2) gives
$$
\lim_{M\to\infty} T_M = a_{N+1}.
$$
Hence the tail converges and
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1}. \tag{3}
$$
As a check, (3) and Step 3 agree: $a_1 = S_N + \sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = (a_1 - a_{N+1}) + a_{N+1}$.

**Step 5: Small tails.** Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $a_n\to 0$, there is an integer $K\ge 1$ such that $|a_k|<\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge K$. Because each $a_k\ge 0$, this says $a_k<\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge K$. Set
$$
N = \max(1,K).
$$
Then $N+1 > K$, so $a_{N+1}<\varepsilon$. By (3),
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.
$$
This proves part 4.

**Remarks on special cases.**

- If $a_1=0$, then $0\le a_n\le a_1=0$ for every $n$, so all $a_n$ are zero and all $d_n$ are zero. Formulas (1) through (3) still hold, since each side is $0$.
- If two consecutive terms are equal, say $a_n=a_{n+1}$, then $d_n=0$. The argument does not require the sequence to decrease strictly. It uses only the telescoping identity (1), which holds whether or not any step is zero.

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with limit zero, and define
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then \(d_n\ge 0\) for every \(n\), the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n\) converges to \(a_1\), and for every integer \(N\ge 1\),
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), some tail after \(N\) terms is less than \(\varepsilon\).

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge 0\). For integers \(M>N\ge 1\), cancellation of consecutive terms gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
&=(a_1-a_2)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1},
\end{aligned}
\qquad
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

As \(N\) increases, \(a_{N+1}\) tends to zero. Thus the first sum tends to \(a_1\), which means the series converges to \(a_1\). For a fixed \(N\), as \(M\) increases, \(a_{M+1}\) tends to zero. The second sum therefore tends to \(a_{N+1}\), giving the stated tail.

Now let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(a_k\to 0\), there is an integer \(K\ge 1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) for all \(k\ge K\). Take \(N=\max(1,K)\). Then \(N+1\ge K\), so the tail is \(a_{N+1}<\varepsilon\).

This also covers \(a_1=0\): nonnegativity and monotonicity then force every \(a_n=0\). If consecutive terms are equal, the corresponding \(d_n\) is zero; strict decrease is not needed.

response:
**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $a_n\to 0$, and put $d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}$. Then:

1. $d_n\ge 0$ for every $n$.
2. The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges, and its sum is $a_1$.
3. For every integer $N\ge 1$, the tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n$ converges and equals $a_{N+1}$.
4. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: the terms are nonnegative.* Since $(a_n)$ is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1}\le a_n$, so
$$
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}\ge 0 .
$$
If $a_n=a_{n+1}$ then $d_n=0$. The argument below never needs a strict decrease.

*Step 2: finite sums telescope.* Fix integers $M>N\ge 1$. Writing out the sum of the first $N$ terms, each $a_k$ with $2\le k\le N$ appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so these cancel in pairs:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$
The same cancellation applies to the terms from $N+1$ through $M$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+(a_{N+2}-a_{N+3})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

*Step 3: the series converges to $a_1$.* By definition, the series converges to a number $S$ when its partial sums $\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n$ tend to $S$ as $N\to\infty$. By (1) the partial sums are $a_1-a_{N+1}$. Because $a_{N+1}\to 0$, we get
$$
\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n=\lim_{N\to\infty}\bigl(a_1-a_{N+1}\bigr)=a_1 .
$$
So $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n=a_1$.

*Step 4: the tail equals $a_{N+1}$.* Fix $N\ge 1$. The tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n$ is the limit, as $M\to\infty$, of the sums $\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n$. By (2), these sums equal $a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}$. Here $a_{N+1}$ is a fixed number and $a_{M+1}\to 0$, so
$$
\lim_{M\to\infty}\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n=\lim_{M\to\infty}\bigl(a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}\bigr)=a_{N+1}.
$$
Hence the tail converges and
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n=a_{N+1}.
$$
This agrees with Step 3 and (1), since $a_1-\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n=a_{N+1}$.

*Step 5: the tail can be made small.* Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $a_k\to 0$, there is an integer $K$ such that $a_k<\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge K$. Take $N=\max(1,K)$. Then $N+1>K$, so by Step 4
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon .
$$

*Remark.* If $a_1=0$, then $0\le a_n\le a_1=0$ for all $n$, so every $a_n$ and every $d_n$ is zero. The identities above still hold in this case. $\blacksquare$

**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $a_n\to0$, and put $d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}$. Then:

1. $d_n\ge0$ for every $n$.
2. $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1$.
3. For every integer $N\ge1$, the tail $\displaystyle\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n$ converges and equals $a_{N+1}$.
4. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: $d_n\ge 0$.* The sequence is nonincreasing, so $a_{n+1}\le a_n$, which gives $d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}\ge0$.

*Step 2: finite sums telescope.* Let $p\le q$ be positive integers. Then

$$
\sum_{n=p}^{q}d_n=(a_p-a_{p+1})+(a_{p+1}-a_{p+2})+\cdots+(a_q-a_{q+1}).
$$

Each of $a_{p+1},\dots,a_q$ appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so these terms cancel. Only $a_p$ and $-a_{q+1}$ remain:

$$
\sum_{n=p}^{q}d_n=a_p-a_{q+1}.\tag{1}
$$

(If $p=q$, this is just the definition of $d_p$.)

*Step 3: the series converges to $a_1$.* A series converges to $s$ if its partial sums converge to $s$. Taking $p=1$ and $q=M$ in (1), the partial sums are

$$
S_M=\sum_{n=1}^{M}d_n=a_1-a_{M+1}.
$$

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $a_n\to0$ and $a_n\ge0$, there is $K$ such that $0\le a_k<\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge K$. For every $M\ge K$ we then have $M+1>K$, so

$$
|S_M-a_1|=a_{M+1}<\varepsilon.
$$

This is the definition of $S_M\to a_1$, so $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1$.

*Step 4: the tail equals $a_{N+1}$.* Fix an integer $N\ge1$. For $M>N$, take $p=N+1$ and $q=M$ in (1). The partial sums of the tail are

$$
T_M=\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
$$

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $K$ as in Step 3. For every $M\ge\max(K,N+1)$,

$$
|T_M-a_{N+1}|=a_{M+1}<\varepsilon.
$$

So the tail series converges, and

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
$$

*Step 5: the tail can be made small.* Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $K$ with $a_k<\varepsilon$ for all $k\ge K$. Put $N=\max(1,K)$. Then $N+1>K$, so by Step 4

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
$$

$\blacksquare$

**Remarks.** If $a_1=0$, then $0\le a_n\le a_1=0$ for all $n$, so every $a_n$ and every $d_n$ is zero. The identities above still hold, with both sides equal to $0$. Strict decrease is never used: if $a_n=a_{n+1}$, then $d_n=0$, which is allowed.

response:
**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) count the \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including neighbors across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), the empty selection is the only selection. The formula also gives
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now suppose \(k\ge 1\). We count valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Every valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible marks, so the number of marked selections is
\[
kA(n,k).
\]

We can also count these marked selections by describing the gaps between selected plots. Choose the starting plot in \(n\) ways, then list the selected plots clockwise from that start. Let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot. The last gap returns to the start, so it includes the circular boundary. When \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

No two selected plots are neighbors precisely when every gap is positive. Since every unselected plot belongs to exactly one gap, we need
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,
\qquad g_i\ge 1.
\]

To count these ordered gap tuples, put \(n-k\) objects in a row. There are \(n-k-1\) internal spaces between consecutive objects. Choosing \(k-1\) of those spaces for separators splits the row into \(k\) nonempty blocks, whose lengths give \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\). Conversely, each such tuple determines exactly those separator positions. Thus the number of tuples is
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
For \(k=1\), we choose no separators and obtain one block, as required.

A starting plot and a gap tuple determine a unique marked selection: move clockwise, leaving \(g_i\) plots unselected before reaching the next selected plot. The \(k\) selected plots and the \(n-k\) unselected plots account for exactly one circuit of the circle. Conversely, a marked selection determines its start and all its gaps. Therefore
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection has been counted exactly once for each of its \(k\) selected plots. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\\
&=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap must be one, which the construction allows. We do not divide by rotations: the plots have fixed, distinct labels, and selections using different labels are different selections. \(\square\)

response:
**Claim.** Let $n \ge 3$ labeled plots be arranged in a circle, and let $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets of plots that contain no two neighboring plots, where plot $n$ and plot $1$ count as neighbors. Then
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*Case $k=0$.* The only selection is the empty set, which has no selected plot. So $A(n,0)=1$. The right-hand side is $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1$, so the formula holds. The empty selection has no plot that can be marked as a start, so it cannot enter the counting below and must be handled separately.

*Case $k\ge 1$.* Let $P$ be the set of pairs $(S,p)$, where $S$ is a valid $k$-selection and $p \in S$ is a marked selected plot. Each valid selection has exactly $k$ choices of marked plot, so
$$
|P| = k\,A(n,k).
$$

We now count $P$ in a second way. Fix the label $p$ of the marked plot. Since the plots have distinct labels, the $n$ possible values of $p$ give disjoint sets of pairs, so $|P|$ is the sum over these $n$ values.

For a fixed $p$, walk clockwise from $p$ and list the selected plots in order as $x_1=p, x_2, \dots, x_k$. Let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $x_i$ and the next selected plot, where $x_{k+1}$ means $x_1=p$ again. When $k=1$, $g_1$ counts the $n-1$ unselected plots between $p$ and itself going around the circle, so $g_1=n-1$.

Two facts about the gaps follow.

- Each $g_i \ge 1$, because no two neighboring plots are both selected.
- $g_1+\dots+g_k = n-k$, because the $k$ selected plots and the $g_i$ unselected plots together make up all $n$ plots.

**The map is a bijection.** Send $(S,p)$ to the pair consisting of $p$ and the gap tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$. Conversely, given $p$ and a tuple of positive integers $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ summing to $n-k$, start at $p$, skip $g_1$ plots clockwise, mark the next plot as $x_2$, skip $g_2$ plots, and continue. After $k$ such steps the walk has covered $n$ plots and returns to $p$. The $k$ marked plots are distinct because each step moves past at least one unselected plot. Reading the gaps off this selection returns the original tuple, and building the selection from the tuple returns the original $S$. So the correspondence is one-to-one in both directions.

**Counting the tuples.** We need the number of ordered $k$-tuples of positive integers with sum $n-k$. Write $n-k$ as a row of $n-k$ unit objects. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between adjacent objects. Choosing $k-1$ of these spaces as cut points splits the row into $k$ nonempty blocks, and each block has a size that is a positive integer. Different cut sets give different tuples, so the count is $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$. This is valid because $k\ge 1$ and $k\le n/2$ give $0 \le k-1 \le n-k-1$.

Therefore, for each of the $n$ labels $p$, there are $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ valid pairs, and
$$
k\,A(n,k) = |P| = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

**Dividing by $k$.** Since $k\ge 1$, we can divide both sides by $k$:
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$
This division is legitimate because $k$ is a fixed positive integer and we are solving an equation. It does not quotient out rotations. The plots have fixed distinct labels, so two selections that differ by a rotation are different sets and are both counted.

**Simplifying.** Since $n-2k\ge 0$, all factorials below are defined:
$$
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$
Also,
$$
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!},
$$
where dividing by $n-k$ is valid because $n-k \ge n/2 > 0$. The two expressions are equal, so
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}. \qquad\blacksquare
$$

**Remark on $k=n/2$.** When $n$ is even and $k=n/2$, the gaps sum to $n-k=k$ and each must be at least $1$. So every gap equals $1$, which is allowed. This matches the count: $\binom{k-1}{k-1}=1$.

response:
**Claim.** Label the $n\ge 3$ plots $1,\dots,n$ and arrange them in a circle, so that plots $n$ and $1$ are neighbors. For an integer $k$ with $0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element sets of plots that contain no two neighboring plots. Then
$$
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*Case $k=0$.* The only $0$-element selection is the empty set. It is valid, so $A(n,0)=1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1$.

*Case $k\ge 1$.* Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of pairs $(S,s)$, where $S$ is a valid $k$-element selection and $s\in S$ is a selected plot marked as the start. Each valid selection $S$ has exactly $k$ selected plots, so it appears in exactly $k$ pairs. Therefore
$$
|\mathcal P| = k\,A(n,k).
$$
Dividing by $k$ is legitimate because $k\ge 1$. It recovers $A(n,k)$ because each unmarked selection is counted once for each of its $k$ selected plots.

Now count $\mathcal P$ in a second way, by first choosing the start $s$. There are $n$ possible labels for $s$. For a fixed $s$, let $\mathcal P_s$ be the set of valid selections containing $s$. We claim that
$$
|\mathcal P_s|=\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\quad\text{for every } s.
$$
Then $|\mathcal P|=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$.

*Encoding by gaps.* Fix $s$ and a valid selection $S\ni s$. Walk clockwise from $s$. Let $g_1$ be the number of unselected plots between $s$ and the next selected plot. For $i=2,\dots,k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots between the $(i-1)$-st and $i$-th selected plots in this order. Then $g_k$ is the number of unselected plots between the last selected plot and $s$. For $k=1$, $g_1=n-1$. Each $g_i$ is at least $1$, because no two selected plots are neighbors. The unselected plots are exactly the plots counted by the gaps, so
$$
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
$$
Let $T$ be the set of ordered $k$-tuples of positive integers with sum $n-k$. The map $S\mapsto(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ sends $\mathcal P_s$ into $T$.

*The map is a bijection.* Given $(g_1,\dots,g_k)\in T$, start at $s$, skip $g_1$ plots, select the next plot, skip $g_2$ plots, select the next plot, and continue in this way. Each round advances $g_i+1$ positions, and the total advance is $\sum_i (g_i+1)=n$. So the walk ends exactly back at $s$, and the $k$ selected plots are distinct. Every gap is at least $1$, so no two selected plots are neighbors, including the pair that meets across the boundary. This gives a valid selection containing $s$ with exactly these gaps. The tuple determines the selection, and the selection determines the tuple, so the map is a bijection.

*Counting $T$.* An element of $T$ is a way to split a row of $n-k$ unselected plots into $k$ nonempty consecutive blocks. The row has $n-k-1$ spaces between neighboring plots. Choosing $k-1$ of those spaces for dividers gives exactly one such split, and every split arises this way. This is the standard stars-and-bars count. The count is nonzero because $k-1\le n-k-1$, which is equivalent to $n\ge 2k$, and this holds since $k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. So
$$
|\mathcal P_s|=|T|=\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Conclusion.* Combining the two counts of $\mathcal P$,
$$
k\,A(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Simplifying.* Using $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}=\dfrac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}$,
$$
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$
Using $\binom{n-k}{k}=\dfrac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}$ and $\dfrac{(n-k)!}{n-k}=(n-k-1)!$,
$$
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$
The two expressions are equal, so $A(n,k)=\dfrac{n}{n-k}\dbinom{n-k}{k}$. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks.**

- At $k=n/2$ for even $n$, $n-2k=0$, and the only gap tuple is $(1,\dots,1)$. The formula gives $A(n,n/2)=n/k=2$, which matches the two alternating selections.
- Check with $n=6$, $k=2$: the formula gives $\frac{6}{4}\binom{4}{2}=9$. Of the $\binom{6}{2}=15$ pairs, $6$ are neighboring pairs, leaving $9$.
- The factor $n$ comes from choosing the start label, not from a rotation quotient. The plots have fixed labels, so two selections that differ by a rotation are different sets, and no division by $n$ is needed.

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) be the number of ways to select \(k\) plots so that no two neighboring plots are selected, including the two plots at the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** When \(k=0\), the only selection is the empty selection, and the formula gives
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now suppose \(k\ge1\). Count pairs consisting of a valid selection and one of its selected plots marked as the start. Each selection gives \(k\) such pairs, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) pairs.

To count the same pairs another way, choose the start plot in \(n\) ways. Starting there and moving clockwise, let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, for \(i=1,\ldots,k\). If \(k=1\), this gap consists of all the other plots before returning to the start. Each \(g_i\) is positive because neighboring plots cannot both be selected, and the gaps contain all \(n-k\) unselected plots. Thus
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
\]

The number of ordered lists of \(k\) positive integers with this sum is \(\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\): represent \(n-k\) as a row of objects and choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) spaces between them as separators. The resulting \(k\) groups give the gap sizes. Each start plot and gap list determines exactly one marked selection, including when the gaps are all one. Hence
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1},
\qquad
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Expanding the factorials gives
\[
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]
The division by \(k\) is legitimate because each valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible choices of the marked plot. The plots have fixed labels, so rotations are not identified. \(\square\)

Together the gaps contain all \(n-k\) unselected plots, so

g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
\]

To count these gap lists, write \(n-k\) objects in a row and place \(k-1\) separators in the \(n-k-1\) spaces between them. Each choice of spaces gives one ordered list of \(k\) positive gap sizes, and every such list comes from exactly one choice of spaces. Thus there are \(\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\) gap lists.

A start plot and its ordered gap list determine exactly one marked selection: take the start, skip \(g_1\) unselected plots, take the next selected plot, and continue around the circle. This also works when \(k=1\), when the single gap accounts for all other plots. Hence
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1},
\qquad
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

\[
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]
The division by \(k\) is legitimate because \(k\ge1\); it corrects for the \(k\) possible marked starts for each selection. At \(k=n/2\) when \(n\) is even, all gaps are one, which satisfies the same count. We do not divide by the number of rotations: the plots have distinct fixed labels.

response:
**Claim.** Arrange $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots in which no two neighboring plots are selected. Plots $n$ and $1$ are neighbors, like any other adjacent pair. Then

$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*The case $k = 0$.* The only selection is the empty one, so $A(n,0) = 1$. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0} = 1$.

*The case $k \ge 1$.* We count marked selections: pairs $(S, s)$ where $S$ is a valid selection of $k$ plots and $s$ is one of the plots in $S$. We count them in two ways.

*First count.* Each valid selection has exactly $k$ choices of marked plot, so the number of marked selections is
$$
k\,A(n,k).
$$

*Second count.* Given $(S,s)$, list the selected plots in clockwise order starting at $s$, as $p_1 = s, p_2, \dots, p_k$, and set $p_{k+1} = p_1$. For $i = 1, \dots, k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ going clockwise. When $k = 1$, $g_1 = n-1$, the number of all other plots. These gaps have two properties:

- Every plot is either selected or lies in exactly one gap, so $g_1 + \dots + g_k = n-k$.
- Every $g_i \ge 1$. For $k = 1$ this holds because $n \ge 3$. For $k \ge 2$, if $g_i = 0$ then $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ would be neighbors, which is forbidden. This includes the pair $p_k, p_1$ when they meet across the boundary between plots $n$ and $1$.

So $(S,s)$ determines a start label $s$ and an ordered tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$.

Conversely, take any start label $s$ and any such tuple. Place the first selected plot at $s$. Then repeat the following for $i = 1, \dots, k-1$: skip $g_i$ plots clockwise and select the next plot. The $k$ selected plots and the $g_1 + \dots + g_{k-1}$ plots skipped so far use up $k + (n-k-g_k) = n - g_k$ consecutive plots starting at $s$. The last $g_k$ plots before returning to $s$ are therefore unselected. The selected plots are distinct, and since every gap is at least $1$, no two of them are neighbors. The result is a valid marked selection, and reading off its start and gaps recovers the original data. Hence marked selections correspond one-to-one with pairs (start label, gap tuple).

There are $n$ start labels. The number of tuples of $k$ positive integers with sum $n-k$ is $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$. To see this, write the $n-k$ unselected plots as a row of $n-k$ objects. There are $n-k-1$ spaces between consecutive objects. Choosing $k-1$ of these spaces for separators cuts the row into $k$ nonempty blocks, and the block sizes form a tuple. Every tuple arises from exactly one choice of separators. Since $k \le n/2$, we have $n-k-1 \ge k-1 \ge 0$, so this binomial coefficient is meaningful. The start label does not affect the number of tuples, so the second count gives $n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ marked selections.

*Dividing by $k$.* Equating the two counts,
$$
k\,A(n,k) = n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$
Each valid selection is counted exactly $k$ times among the marked selections, once for each choice of marked plot. Since $k \ge 1$, we may divide by $k$:
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Rewriting the coefficient.* Expanding the binomial coefficient,
$$
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
= \frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$
On the other hand, since $n-k \ge n/2 > 0$,
$$
\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}
= \frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}
= \frac{n\,(n-k-1)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}.
$$
The two expressions agree, so $A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}$. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks.**

1. When $n$ is even and $k = n/2$, the sum $n-k = k$ forces every gap to equal $1$. This is allowed, because gaps only need to be positive. The formula gives $\frac{n}{n/2}\binom{n/2}{n/2} = 2$, matching the two alternating selections.
2. We never divide by rotations of the circle. The plots have distinct fixed labels, so selections that differ by a rotation are different selections, and the $n$ choices of start label are all counted.

**Claim.** Place $n \ge 3$ labeled garden plots around a circle. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $A(n,k)$ be the number of $k$-element selections of plots in which no two selected plots are neighbors. The plots at the circular boundary (plot $n$ and plot $1$) count as neighbors. Then
$$
A(n,k) = \frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
$$

**Proof.**

*The case $k=0$.* There is exactly one empty selection, and it has no pair of selected plots, so it is valid. Hence $A(n,0)=1$. The formula also gives $\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1$. The argument below needs a selected plot to mark, so it covers only $k\ge 1$.

*Step 1: count selections with a marked plot.* Now let $k \ge 1$. Call a pair $(S,s)$ a *marked selection* if $S$ is a valid selection of $k$ plots and $s\in S$. Each valid selection has exactly $k$ choices of $s$, and different choices give different pairs. So the number of marked selections is
$$
k\,A(n,k).
$$
We count the marked selections a second way and then divide by $k$.

*Step 2: record a marked selection by its starting plot and its gaps.* Given $(S,s)$, let $p$ be the label of $s$. Starting at $s$ and moving clockwise, list the selected plots as $s_1=s, s_2,\dots,s_k$, and put $s_{k+1}=s_1$. For $i=1,\dots,k$, let $g_i$ be the number of unselected plots strictly between $s_i$ and $s_{i+1}$. For $k=1$, the only gap $g_1$ consists of the other $n-1$ plots, all the way around the circle back to $s_1$.

These numbers satisfy two conditions.

- Each $g_i\ge 1$. Two selected plots are never neighbors, so at least one unselected plot lies between consecutive selected plots. For $i=k$, the gap runs from $s_k$ around the circular boundary back to $s_1$, so the condition on the boundary pair is included.
- $g_1+\dots+g_k=n-k$. Every unselected plot lies in exactly one gap, and there are $n-k$ unselected plots.

So $(S,s)$ determines a pair consisting of a starting label $p\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$ of positive integers with sum $n-k$.

*Step 3: the correspondence can be reversed.* Take any label $p$ and any positive integers $g_1,\dots,g_k$ with sum $n-k$. Select plot $p$. Move clockwise past $g_1$ unselected plots and select the next plot. Then move past $g_2$ unselected plots and select the next, and so on. Each selected plot together with the gap after it uses $g_i+1$ plots, and these total $\sum_i (g_i+1)=n$. So after $k$ selections we have gone around the circle exactly once and arrive back at $p$. The $k$ selected plots are therefore distinct. Every gap, including the last one before $p$, contains at least one plot, so no two selected plots are neighbors, even across the boundary. This gives a valid selection with $p$ marked, and its gaps are the $g_i$ we started with. Steps 2 and 3 undo each other, so marked selections correspond one-to-one with pairs (starting label, gap tuple).

*Step 4: count the pairs.* There are $n$ choices of starting label. The tuples are compositions of $n-k$ into $k$ positive parts. To count them, write the $n-k$ unselected plots in a row. This row has $n-k-1$ spaces between consecutive plots. Choosing $k-1$ of these spaces as cuts splits the row into $k$ nonempty blocks, and the block sizes form a tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_k)$. Different choices of cuts give different tuples, and every tuple arises this way. So there are $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ tuples. Since $k\le n/2$, we have $n-k-1\ge k-1$, and the binomial coefficient is the correct count, including $k=1$, where it equals $1$. Combining Steps 1 to 4,
$$
k\,A(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Step 5: divide by $k$.* The division by $k$ is legitimate because every valid selection appears in exactly $k$ marked selections, one for each choice of marked plot. We do not divide by $n$. The plots have distinct fixed labels, so selections that differ by a rotation are different selections and are counted separately. Therefore
$$
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
$$

*Step 6: rewrite the coefficient.* Here $n-k\ge 2$ and $n-2k\ge 0$, so all factorials below are defined. Expanding,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
&=\frac{n}{k}\cdot\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)\,(n-k-1)!}{k\,(k-1)!\,(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\cdot\frac{(n-k)!}{k!\,(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This proves the claim. For the largest value of $k$ with $n$ even, $k=n/2$, every gap equals $1$. This is allowed, and there are $n/2 \cdot \frac{2}{1}\binom{n/2-1}{n/2-1}=2$ valid selections, namely the two alternating ones. $\qquad\blacksquare$

The compost thermometer has returned from its brief career as a dibber. It is back on the hook inside the shed, where it can resume measuring temperature rather than making holes. Please use the wooden dibbers for planting. They have fewer opinions about heat.

This month we are comparing the middle of the active heap with its outer edge. On your rota day, take one reading at each marked position and record both on the sheet. Push the probe to the mark on its shaft, wait until the display settles, and wipe it before returning it to the hook. If the display never settles, write that down instead of choosing the number you like best.

A warmer middle is interesting, but a single pair of readings will not tell us whether the whole heap is ready to use. We are collecting observations over the month. The stewards will also inspect the material before deciding whether to open the bay for collection. Until the notice changes, please keep adding suitable material to the active bay and leave the resting bay alone.

The recording sheet has room for comments because weather, recently added material, and an uncooperative display may help explain a reading. You do not need to write a small novel. “Heavy rain this morning” is useful. “The heap has entered a troubled period” is less useful, though we appreciate the concern.

**Map Archive: Changes to Retrieval During the Trial**

For the next six weeks, the map archive will change how it retrieves requested material. The reading room will keep its usual opening hours, and access to the collection is unchanged. Only retrieval is affected: until now, readers have sometimes assumed that any item could be brought up immediately, which is no longer the case.

Requests received before noon will be collected and retrieved together at two o'clock. There will be no second afternoon retrieval during the trial.

You do not need to arrive before noon. If you have requested a map in advance, you can come in later. If you arrive later without a request, you can still use the catalogues and open shelves, and you can submit a request for the next opening day. What matters is that the request reaches us before noon, not that you do. Each request must include a shelfmark. Requests without one will be held while staff help identify the item, and they will join the next retrieval after identification. That may not be the day the request was first received.

Some maps have already been identified as fragile. These require a support prepared by the conservation team. The conservation team will contact you to arrange an appointment, and the two o'clock retrieval does not apply to these appointments. The catalogue will mark affected maps. If an item is found to need support during retrieval, staff will contact you.

The trial is meant to reduce interruptions in the store. It does not reduce opening hours. We will count delayed requests and review reader comments before deciding whether to continue. A comment card is available at the desk throughout the trial.

# Map Archive: Trial Retrieval Arrangements

For the next six weeks, the map archive is trying a different arrangement for retrieving material. The reading room will keep its usual opening times. Only retrieval changes, not access. Being able to use the archive has sometimes been taken to mean that every item can be brought upstairs immediately, and during the trial that will not always be the case.

## How to request a map

Requests received before noon will be collected together and retrieved at two. There will be no second afternoon retrieval during the trial.

You do not need to arrive before noon. Only the request has to arrive by then, and it must include a shelfmark. If you have requested a map in advance, you can arrive later and use it. If you arrive later without a request, you can still use the catalogues and open shelves, and you can submit a request for the next opening day.

A request without a shelfmark will be held while staff help you identify the item. It will join the next retrieval after the item is identified, which may not be on the day we first received it.

## Fragile maps

Maps already identified as fragile need a support prepared by the conservation team. The team will contact you with an appointment, and the two o'clock retrieval does not apply to these appointments. The catalogue shows which maps are affected. If an item turns out to need support during retrieval, staff will contact you.

## About the trial

The trial is intended to reduce interruptions in the store. It does not reduce opening hours. Before deciding whether to continue, we will count delayed requests and review reader comments. A comment card will be available at the desk throughout the trial.

The amber indicator on the curing-line monitor appeared just after washdown on three of the last five morning shifts. It means the humidity probe’s reading is outside the range accepted by the controller, but it does not tell us whether the room is too humid or the probe’s reading is unreliable. The other display, often called the backup, measures temperature only. A normal reading there cannot resolve a question about humidity.

On all three mornings, the amber light cleared within twelve minutes. Operators wiped moisture from the outside of the probe housing on two mornings. On the third, nobody touched it. These observations are consistent with moisture around the housing, but they do not establish that wiping cleared the warning. The housing is not the sensing element. Wiping is recorded here as an observation, not a recommended remedy.

For now, record when the indicator appears, when it clears, and whether washdown has finished. Do not open the housing. If the indicator remains amber after fifteen minutes, call the shift lead before starting the next batch. The lead may request a handheld humidity check using the unit in the instrument cabinet. A handheld reading does not authorize a restart. The shift lead must make that decision.

Maintenance has been asked to inspect the seal at the next planned stop, but this does not establish that the seal has failed. Continue recording mornings with no warning by marking the “no warning” box beside the time fields. We need those entries as well as the warnings to determine how often the pattern occurs.

response:
Rain may affect a recording before it affects the animals whose calls we hope to count. This matters when comparing wet and dry surveys. A change in the count could also reflect a change in calling, but that is the ecological quantity of interest only if the question concerns calling. Our pilot therefore asked whether a rain shield changes the output of one fixed call detector. We did not try to estimate the number of animals.

We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, one shielded and one exposed, with positions within a patch assigned by a coin toss. The two devices recorded simultaneously. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, giving 144 paired windows. From the field log, 48 windows were classified as wet and 96 as dry. Weather was not assigned. A window was counted as positive when the detector marked at least one target call, and the detector settings were the same throughout.

In wet windows, the devices agreed in 29 of 48 pairs. The shielded device alone was positive in twelve pairs and the exposed device alone in seven. In dry windows, the devices agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with five shield-only positives and seven exposed-only positives. Agreement covers pairs in which both devices were positive and pairs in which neither was, and we have not separated the two in this summary. The agreement counts therefore should not be read as the number of windows with calls.

The excess of shield-only over exposed-only positives in wet windows is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain. It does not show that the shield recovered genuine calls, because calls were not independently labeled. It also does not show that rain reduced calling. In addition, windows within a patch are repeated measurements, so 144 is not the number of independent ecological replicates. Because weather was observed rather than assigned, any difference between wet and dry windows is also not attributable to rain alone. These limitations do not make the paired comparison uninformative about disagreement between the devices.

The pilot identifies a measurement question to examine before these recordings are used for an ecological trend. A next study could add blinded human labeling and more patches, but it has not been run. For the present data, we can report the direction of discordance and how it differs between the observed weather categories, and the biological interpretation remains open.

We introduced the persistence rule because a single pressure spike need not indicate a valve fault. It requires two threshold crossings within a cycle before raising an alarm. The comparison rule uses a higher threshold and alarms after one crossing. Both thresholds and the persistence requirement were fixed using a separate setup recording, without using the evaluation recordings. Because the rules differ in both threshold and persistence requirement, the comparison does not isolate the effect of persistence. The lower threshold also changes which cycles can produce an alarm.

The held-out bench set contains 120 cycles from one machine: 30 with an induced valve fault and 90 with no induced fault. Each rule produces at most one alarm per cycle. The persistence rule alarms in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and eight of the 90 no-fault cycles. The comparison rule alarms in 21 fault cycles and three no-fault cycles. The persistence rule therefore detects more induced faults in this set, at the cost of more alarms in cycles designated no-fault. Here, “no-fault” means that no fault was induced. We did not dismantle the machine after every cycle to exclude every possible defect.

Eighteen fault cycles trigger both rules. Comparing delays on shared detections keeps the set of cycles the same for both rules, but excludes faults detected by only one rule and faults missed by both. The delay result applies only to this shared subset.

Although transient spikes motivated the persistence rule, its observed benefit was higher detection of induced faults, accompanied by more alarms in no-fault cycles. Combining a low threshold with a persistence requirement does not by itself establish better false-alarm control.

These recordings evaluate two fixed rules under one bench arrangement. They do not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. We have not selected a preferred rule because the acceptable tradeoff depends on the costs of missing a fault and interrupting a cycle, which were not measured.

The persistence rule alarms in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and in 8 of the 90 no-fault cycles. The comparison rule alarms in 21 fault cycles and 3 no-fault cycles. In this set, then, the persistence rule detects more of the induced faults and also alarms more often in the no-fault cycles. Here "no-fault" means only that no fault was induced. We did not dismantle the machine after every cycle to exclude every possible defect.

Eighteen fault cycles trigger both rules. On those cycles, the mean time from the logged fault onset to the first alarm is 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule and 2.8 seconds for the comparison rule. Restricting the delay comparison to shared detections means both means are taken over the same cycles. It also leaves out the faults that only one rule detects. The persistence rule alone detects 6 of the faults and the comparison rule alone detects 3, which leaves 3 faults that neither rule detects. The delay result therefore holds only for the 18 shared detections.

The rule was motivated by transient spikes, but what we observed was higher detection of induced faults at the cost of more alarms in no-fault cycles. A lower threshold combined with a persistence condition is not, by its construction alone, evidence of better false-alarm control, and these results do not show it.

These recordings test two fixed rules under one bench arrangement. They do not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. We have not selected a preferred rule, because the acceptable tradeoff depends on the cost of a missed fault and the cost of interrupting a cycle, and we did not measure either.

response:
We propose revising the short discovery labels attached to twenty digitized collections. Some labels repeat terms from old inventory headings without explaining whose categories those were. These labels help readers decide which collection to open and form part of how the archive represents its collections. Changing them would change the archive’s present description, while leaving the scanned inventories available exactly as they are.

The existing labels offer a retrieval benefit: readers following a quotation from an inventory can recognize the same words in the catalogue. But readers who have not seen the inventory may take the discovery label as the archive’s present description. Repeating an old heading can therefore help one reader find a collection while misleading another about how the archive describes it.

To accommodate both uses, we propose a current descriptive label, a note identifying the original heading, and the original heading retained as a searchable alternative. response:
Let \(A\ge 0\), let \(c_0\in\mathbb R\), and suppose the real corrections \(\delta_k\) satisfy
\[
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}
\qquad\text{for every integer }k\ge 0.
\]
Define the cumulative corrected values by
\[
c_n=c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k,
\qquad n\ge 0,
\]
where the sum is empty when \(n=0\). We will show that \(c_n\) converges to a finite real limit \(c\) and that
\[
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}
\qquad\text{for every integer }m\ge 0.
\]

\[

**Claim.** Let $A\ge 0$, let $c_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\delta_k\in\mathbb R$ for each integer $k\ge 0$, with
$$
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}\qquad(k\ge 0).
$$
Define $c_n=c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k$ for $n\ge 1$, and $c_0$ for $n=0$, where the empty sum is zero. Then there is a real number $c$ with $c_n\to c$, and
$$
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}\qquad\text{for every integer } m\ge 0.
$$
The corrections may have either sign. The argument uses only their absolute values.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: Partial fractions.* For each $k\ge 0$,
$$
\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}=\frac{(k+2)-(k+1)}{(k+1)(k+2)}=\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}.
$$

*Step 2: A bound on tails.* Let $n>m\ge 0$. In $c_n-c_m$, the constant $c_0$ cancels, and so do the terms $\delta_k$ with $k<m$. Therefore
$$
c_n-c_m=\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k.
$$
By the triangle inequality and the hypothesis on $\delta_k$,
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}.
$$
By Step 1, the sum telescopes. Each term $-\frac{1}{k+2}$ cancels the term $\frac{1}{(k+1)+1}$ from the next index, so only the first and last terms survive:
$$
A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right).
$$
The last term is $-\frac{1}{(n-1)+2}=-\frac{1}{n+1}$. Since $A\ge 0$ and $\frac{1}{n+1}>0$, we get
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\le \frac{A}{m+1}\qquad(n>m\ge 0). \tag{1}
$$

*Step 3: The sequence is Cauchy.* Let $\varepsilon>0$. Because $A/(M+1)\to 0$ as $M\to\infty$, there is an integer $M\ge 0$ with $A/(M+1)<\varepsilon$. (If $A=0$, any $M$ works.) Take integers $p,q\ge M$, and set $m=\min(p,q)$ and $n=\max(p,q)$.

- If $p=q$, then $|c_p-c_q|=0<\varepsilon$.
- If $p\ne q$, then $n>m\ge M$, and by (1),
$$
|c_p-c_q|=|c_n-c_m|\le\frac{A}{m+1}\le\frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon.
$$

So $(c_n)$ is Cauchy. Since $\mathbb R$ is complete, there is a real number $c$ with $c_n\to c$.

*Step 4: The error bound.* Fix $m\ge 0$. By (1), $|c_n-c_m|\le A/(m+1)$ for every $n>m$. The left side is a continuous function of $c_n$, and $c_n\to c$, so $|c_n-c_m|\to|c-c_m|$ as $n\to\infty$. Non-strict inequalities survive limits, so
$$
|c-c_m|\le\frac{A}{m+1}.
$$

*Remark on $A=0$.* In this case the hypothesis forces $\delta_k=0$ for all $k$. Then $c_n=c_0$ for every $n$, so $c=c_0$, and the bound reads $|c_0-c_m|=0\le 0$. This agrees with the general argument.

**Proposition.** Let $A\ge 0$, let $c_0\in\mathbb R$, and for each integer $k\ge 0$ let $\delta_k\in\mathbb R$ satisfy

$$
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}.
$$

Define $c_n = c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k$ for $n\ge 1$, and $c_0$ at $n=0$ (the empty sum). Then $c_n$ has a finite real limit $c$, and

$$
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}\qquad\text{for every integer } m\ge 0.
$$

**Proof.**

*Step 1: a telescoping identity.* For every integer $k\ge 0$,

$$
\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}=\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2},
$$

because the right-hand side equals $\dfrac{(k+2)-(k+1)}{(k+1)(k+2)}$. Summing over $k$ from $m$ to $n-1$ for integers $n>m\ge 0$, the term $-\frac{1}{k+2}$ at index $k$ cancels the term $\frac{1}{k+2}$ at index $k+1$. Only the first and last terms survive:

$$
\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}
=\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)
=\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}.
$$

*Step 2: a bound on tails.* Let $n>m\ge 0$. Subtracting the definitions of $c_n$ and $c_m$ leaves only the corrections with indices from $m$ to $n-1$:

$$
c_n-c_m=\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k.
$$

The triangle inequality, the hypothesis on each $\delta_k$, and Step 1 give

$$
\begin{aligned}
|c_n-c_m|
&=\left|\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k\right|\\
&\le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|\\
&\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}\\
&=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A\ge 0$ and $\frac{1}{n+1}>0$, the last expression is at most $\frac{A}{m+1}$. Therefore

$$
|c_n-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}\qquad\text{whenever } n>m\ge 0. \tag{$*$}
$$

Note that this estimate uses only the absolute values $|\delta_k|$. The signs of the corrections and the monotonicity of the partial sums play no role.

*Step 3: the sequence is Cauchy.* Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $A/(M+1)\to 0$ as $M\to\infty$ (by the Archimedean property of $\mathbb R$), choose an integer $M\ge 0$ with

$$
\frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon.
$$

Let $p,q\ge M$. If $p=q$, then $|c_q-c_p|=0<\varepsilon$. If $p\ne q$, by symmetry we may assume $q>p$. Applying $(*)$ with $m=p$ and $n=q$, and using $p+1\ge M+1$ together with $A\ge 0$,

$$
|c_q-c_p|\le \frac{A}{p+1}\le \frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon.
$$

Thus $(c_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence. By the completeness of $\mathbb R$, it converges to some real number $c$. In particular, $c$ is finite.

*Step 4: the error bound.* Fix an integer $m\ge 0$. By $(*)$, $|c_n-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}$ for every $n>m$. The function $x\mapsto |x-c_m|$ is continuous, so $|c_n-c_m|\to|c-c_m|$ as $n\to\infty$. A limit of quantities bounded by $\frac{A}{m+1}$ is bounded by $\frac{A}{m+1}$, so

$$
|c-c_m|=\lim_{n\to\infty}|c_n-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}. \qquad\blacksquare
$$

**Remark.** If $A=0$, every correction satisfies $\delta_k=0$, so $c_n=c_0$ for all $n$. The argument above covers this case, and it gives $c=c_0$ with error bound $0$.

**Claim.** Let $A\ge 0$ and $c_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\delta_k\in\mathbb R$ for every integer $k\ge 0$ satisfy
$$
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)} .
$$
Define $c_n=c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k$ for $n\ge 1$, and $c_0$ is the value at $n=0$ (the empty sum). Then $c_n$ converges to a real number $c$, and
$$
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}\qquad\text{for every integer } m\ge 0 .
$$
The corrections $\delta_k$ may have either sign.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: a bound on the difference of two partial sums.* Let $n>m\ge 0$. Subtracting the two definitions leaves only the terms with indices $m,\dots,n-1$, so
$$
c_n-c_m=\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k .
$$
Taking absolute values and applying the triangle inequality and the hypothesis on $\delta_k$ gives
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)} .
$$
The summand telescopes because
$$
\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}=\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
|c_n-c_m|
&\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)\\
&=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\\
&\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$

*Step 2: the sequence is Cauchy.* Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $A/(M+1)\to 0$ as $M\to\infty$, we can choose an integer $M\ge 0$ with $A/(M+1)<\varepsilon$. Take $n>m\ge M$. By (1),
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}\le \frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon .
$$
If instead $m>n\ge M$, exchange the roles of $m$ and $n$ and use $|c_n-c_m|=|c_m-c_n|$ to get the same bound. If $m=n$ the difference is $0<\varepsilon$. Hence $|c_n-c_m|<\varepsilon$ for all $m,n\ge M$, so $(c_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence. Since $\mathbb R$ is complete, there is a real number $c$ with $c_n\to c$.

*Step 3: the error bound.* Fix $m\ge 0$. The first two lines of (1) hold for every $n>m$:
$$
|c_n-c_m|\le A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right).
$$
Let $n\to\infty$. Since $c_n\to c$ and the absolute value is continuous, the left side tends to $|c-c_m|$. The right side tends to $A/(m+1)$. A non-strict inequality between convergent sequences is preserved in the limit, so
$$
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
$$
Since $m$ was arbitrary, this holds for every $m\ge 0$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Remarks.** If $A=0$, then every $\delta_k=0$, so $c_n=c_0$ for all $n$ and $c=c_0$. The argument assumes no monotonicity of the corrections or of the partial sums. It controls only the absolute size of the tails $\sum_{k\ge m}\delta_k$, and this is why corrections of either sign are allowed.

There are \(n\) labeled exhibit stations and \(n\) labeled tour groups, both indexed by \(1,\ldots,n\). Each group visits exactly one station, and each station receives exactly one group. Thus a schedule is a permutation \(\pi\), where group \(i\) visits station \(\pi(i)\). A schedule is **clear** if
\[
\pi(i)\ne i \qquad\text{for every }i.
\]
The matching labels designate pairings to avoid. They do not describe physical positions, and the stations need not be arranged in a line or circle.

For every integer \(n\ge 0\), the number \(D_n\) of clear schedules is
\[
D_n
=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!
=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
\]
We use \(0!=1\) and include the unique empty schedule when \(n=0\).

To prove the formula, we assign each schedule a weight that is one if it is clear and zero otherwise. For a fixed schedule \(\pi\), let
\[
F(\pi)=\{i:\pi(i)=i\}
\]
be the set of labels whose pairings we wanted to avoid. Consider the weight
\[
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}.
\]
If \(F(\pi)\) is empty, its only subset is the empty set, which contributes one. If \(F(\pi)\) has \(m\ge 1\) members, it has \(\binom{m}{k}\) subsets of size \(k\), so
\[
\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}
=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\binom{m}{k}(-1)^k
=(1-1)^m
=0.
\]
Thus summing these weights over all schedules counts exactly the clear schedules.

We can now count the same contributions by choosing \(S\) first. Since all sums are finite, we may change their order:
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_n
&=\sum_{\pi}\ \sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}\\
&=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}
(-1)^{|S|}\,\#\{\pi:S\subseteq F(\pi)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For a given subset \(S\) of size \(k\), the condition \(S\subseteq F(\pi)\) requires each group with a label in \(S\) to visit the station with that same label. This uses those \(k\) groups and stations. The remaining \(n-k\) groups can be assigned bijectively to the remaining \(n-k\) stations in \((n-k)!\) ways.

These assignments may also pair a group outside \(S\) with its matching station. Such schedules must be included: the condition requires the labels in \(S\) to be fixed, without forbidding other fixed labels. The alternating weights ensure that every schedule with any fixed labels contributes zero overall.

There are \(\binom{n}{k}\) choices of \(S\) with size \(k\). Grouping the terms by this size gives
\[
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!.
\]
Finally,
\[
\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!
=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}(n-k)!
=\frac{n!}{k!},
\]
which gives the second formula.

When \(n=0\), the empty schedule has no pairings to avoid, and the formula gives \(D_0=1\). When \(n=1\), the only schedule pairs group \(1\) with station \(1\), so \(D_1=0\). When \(n=2\), the sole clear schedule swaps the assignments: group \(1\) visits station \(2\), and group \(2\) visits station \(1\).
